factsAccepted: Platform uptime is 99.2%, below industry standard for SaaS of 99.9%+. Incident frequency: 2-3 incidents per month with average 2-hour resolution time. Recent incidents: 4-hour outage on data sync (critical workflow path), 8-minute page load times during peak usage (weekly during month-end when customers are busy). These are not rare events; customers are experiencing reliability issues monthly.

Churn rate increased from 2% MRR (6 months ago) to 3% MRR (current). While 3% MRR is within SaaS norms, the trend is concerning. At 3% MRR, annualized churn is ~35%. Customer interviews (sample of 8 churned customers, 5 at-risk customers) consistently cite reliability and performance issues as switching drivers: 'We can't rely on the platform for critical workflows,' 'Page load times make it unusable during month-end,' 'We had an outage that disrupted our operations.' Feature gaps mentioned by <20% of interview subjects; reliability mentioned by >60%.

NPS is 42 (low for SaaS; healthy range 40-70, world-class >70). NPS survey open-ended feedback: detractors (20% of responses) specifically mention 'product reliability,' 'system crashes,' 'performance issues during busy times.' Promoters (40%) mention 'core workflow automation features are excellent' and 'good support team,' but reliability concerns prevent them from enthusiastically recommending. The gap between feature quality (high satisfaction) and reliability (low NPS) suggests a product-quality issue, not a feature gap.

Support ticket volume increased 40% YoY (from estimated 150 to 210 tickets/month), while customer base grew 20% YoY (180 to 150 customers). This means support tickets per customer are increasing, suggesting growing customer frustration or product issues generating more support inquiries. Average support resolution time trending up (was 16 hours, now 24 hours), indicating either more complex issues or resource constraint. Support team (4 people) is at capacity; hiring more support staff without fixing underlying product issues is treating symptom, not cause.

Two well-funded competitors entered market in past 12 months with features comparable to current product and 99.99% uptime SLAs. These entrants have $50M+ combined funding and are acquiring customers at rates suggesting competitive win-rates. Company's competitive advantage is now questioned: not feature differentiation (entrants have comparable features) and not reliability (entrants have superior uptime). Customers are in evaluation mode comparing reliability and feature parity, not choosing based on company's current strengths.

Customer willingness-to-pay for reliability vs features (not surveyed)
Competitive feature parity analysis (subjective assessment only)
Detailed technical debt inventory (not formally documented)
